Jensen Huang has spent years building Nvidia [NASDAQ: NVDA] into a tech giant, while making himself one of the richest people in the world along the way. Now, an affair could threaten more than just his reputation. In a letter to Nvidia employees, Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife following reports that he had a relationship with Alice Huang (who has no relation to the Nvidia CEO), a former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, who U.S. authorities reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Nvidia's board has since launched an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence, but the affair could also have major consequences for his personal fortune. His wife, Lori, is a co-trustee of a family trust that includes more than 528 million Nvidia shares as of March 2026, according to the company's 2026 proxy statement. If this scandal were to lead to a divorce, billions of dollars could potentially be at stake. According to The New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the preparation of a classified memo earlier this spring, which reportedly warned senior Trump administration officials about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang. The memo was based on electronic surveillance of Alice, whom U.S. officials believed had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency. Nvidia makes some of the world's most advanced AI chips, which power everything from chatbots to data centres. The U.S. has restricted sales of certain chips to China over concerns that the technology could be used to strengthen the rival country's military and AI capabilities. Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it's raising alarm bells for older investors Megaspeed, where Alice worked as an executive, reportedly purchased about $2 billion worth of Nvidia products in recent years, the NYT reports. U.S. authorities also suspect Megaspeed helped get restricted chips into China, bypassing U.S. export rules. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," Nvidia's board of directors said in a statement. The board also said it still has confidence in Huang's leadership, and he has agreed to cooperate with the investigation. "Today's news will not slow Nvidia," an company spokesperson told Moneywise. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." Huang and his wife were college sweethearts who studied engineering together at Oregon State University. The couple married in 1985, eight years before Huang co-founded Nvidia, and have since built a life and an enormous fortune together. Huang, however, has already seen billions wiped off his fortune in recent days. On Nov. 5, his net worth fell by $15.1 billion to $150.9 billion as Nvidia shares plunged more than 9% amid broader concerns about AI spending. That decline came before Huang publicly admitted to the affair. His fortune took another hit Nov. 9 following news of the investigation, as Nvidia shares were down 5% at 11 a.m. EST. In fact, Forbes estimates Huang lost $7.4 billion within the first half-hour of trading. But if Huang and his wife were to divorce, there could be even more money at stake. They have long-standing ties to California, where assets acquired during a marriage are generally considered community property and typically divided equally between spouses. Huang founded Nvidia after the couple married, which means some of his enormous wealth could potentially be subject to division. However, the outcome would depend on how the assets are owned, the terms of their trusts and whether they have any marital agreements. Since California is a no-fault divorce state, an affair alone wouldn't generally entitle Lori to a larger share of their wealth. For now, Lori hasn't publicly commented on the affair and there's no indication the couple is planning to divorce. In his apology, Huang said he hopes his family can heal and that, over time, he can earn back their trust. Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang admitted in a Nov. 8 memo to employees to an affair following reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials believe worked for China's Ministry of State Security. "I was unfaithful to my wife," he wrote. The board has opened an independent investigation. Nvidia stock fell about 4% Monday to its lowest close since April, even as the PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) jumped nearly 7%. That's its worst showing against the chip index since January 2019, by Yahoo Finance calculations. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. The scale is hard to overstate. At Friday's close, Nvidia was worth about four times the nine biggest companies ever hit by CEO personal-conduct scandals combined, by Yahoo Finance calculations. The largest, Intel (INTC), was worth $249 billion when Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 over a past consensual relationship with an employee. Nvidia was about 18 times that. This is key-person risk — the danger that a company's value rests on one person — at its most extreme. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has run it ever since, with no named successor. Adjust for a bigger stock market, and the gap narrows but doesn't close. No earlier scandal-hit company made up more than about 1% of the S&P 500, a mark only Intel in 2018 and HP (HPQ) in 2010 reached. Nvidia is about seven times that. History puts a price on it. A 2018 study in the Journal of Financial Economics found stocks fell about 4% on average when the CEO was the one caught. At Nvidia's size, that's roughly $185 billion, more than McDonald's (MCD) was worth when it fired Steve Easterbrook in 2019. Nvidia lost about $190 billion in market value Monday. Until Monday, Wall Street had treated Nvidia like the safe chip stock. Through Friday's close, Nvidia had fallen about 13% since Oct. 28, the last close before The New York Times' first spy report. The chip index dropped about 20% over that stretch, which included a post-midterm rout. Spy stories can hit hard. Super Micro Computer (SMCI) lost 41% in a day in 2018 on a report of Chinese spy chips in its servers, a report that was never confirmed. The closer precedent may be Intel's Lip-Bu Tan. In August 2025, President Trump said Tan should resign over Tan's China ties. Within a month, Washington had taken a stake in Intel, and the stock was up about 20%. This time, Trump is in the CEO's corner. "I think he's an honorable guy," he told reporters Sunday. That could become its own problem. The bigger questions in Congress "are going to be about Nvidia's relationship with Trump and Trump's relationship with Nvidia," Chris Miller, a professor at Tufts University's Fletcher School and author of "Chip War," told Yahoo Finance on Monday. "If it's true that the president had this intelligence for some time, but declined to act on it, that will be a focus of investigation," he said. Options traders are bracing for more. Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17, and the next day the Republican chairs of three House committees want Huang at a closed-door briefing. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Nvidia (NVDA) stock's sell-off looks overdone to me, ahead of Q3 earnings. The artificial intelligence (AI) computing giant remains about 22% below its 52-week high after Friday's premarket rebound. Yet CEO Jensen Huang reminded us just two weeks ago that "Demand is extraordinary. Capacity is the constraint." That hardly describes a business losing any momentum. I believe political uncertainty deserves attention, but recent deployments suggest the global buildout continues. With Fiscal 2028 earnings valued around 12x at today's share price, I think the decline offers an unusually attractive entry point. Thus, my NVDA stock forecast remains bullish. Nvidia's Q3 could deliver another beat when it reports on November 17. Consensus calls for $108.8 billion of revenue and $2.47 earnings per share (EPS), against management's $108 billion revenue midpoint, plus or minus 2%. Q2 revenue surged 106% to $96.2 billion, with Data Center increasing 117% to $89 billion. Consensus sits less than 1% above guidance, leaving room for stronger deliveries. Nvidia held about $32 billion of inventory while preparing for Rubin's launch. Converting that investment into system deliveries could help revenue beat guidance. Production shipments began during Q3, and management expects Rubin to contribute about 20% of quarterly Data Center revenue. We are also looking at Neoclouds expanding to serve enterprises and sovereign customers. Management expects those buyers to drive sequential growth, with hyperscaler growth reaccelerating afterward as Rubin supply improves. I'll be watching shipment conversion closely because customers can't generate revenue until Nvidia delivers the equipment. Gross margins need attention too. Management expects 74% in Q3, down from 75%, as memory costs surge. Q4 could fall to 71%–72%. Those remain exceptional margins, and higher volumes can support earnings despite the pressure. Guidance also assumes no China Data Center compute revenue. Any permitted sales could help, although I wouldn't rely on them. Now, I believe Nvidia's growth will extend beyond this upcoming quarter. Several recent announcements point in that direction. Oracle's (ORCL) October 27 expansion targets multi-gigawatt Vera Rubin infrastructure. Google's (GOOGL) A5X infrastructure is designed to scale to 960,000 Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs) across multiple sites, with general availability planned this month. These are long-term deployment plans. Meanwhile, Meta (META) is expanding Rubin and Vera central processing unit (CPU) deployments around Muse. Those plans support demand beyond training. Running agents and improving models through reinforcement learning require substantial compute. Physical AI also adds robotics workloads. Nvidia also captures spending on networking and CPUs alongside GPUs, while Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) supports customers across hardware generations. The physical rollout should improve too. DSX POD modular factories can be installed in as little as 14 days, with deliveries planned for early 2027. That applies to prepared sites with supporting infrastructure. Of course, it doesn't eliminate permitting or power requirements. Still, faster installation helps turn spending into usable capacity. Management expects roughly 70% Fiscal 2028 revenue growth, with supply constrained through that year. It's also worth mentioning that October's capacity agreements target a 2.5x substrate expansion over three years. Manufacturing partners are making long-term commitments to meet Nvidia's requirements. Expansion is increasingly global. Google is adding European availability, while Saudi Arabia's HUMAIN plans further Blackwell and Rubin deployments. I believe this gives Nvidia customers outside the U.S. a construction cycle. Now, to be fair, the Democratic congressional sweep has intensified regulatory fears. This is especially true around electricity costs and development restrictions. However, Congress generally doesn't approve individual data centers. Zoning decisions usually sit locally, while environmental permitting and grid connections involve separate authorities. State leadership therefore matters. So, sure, Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa wants development paused pending protections, and local ballot measures favored restrictions. Delays could hurt deliveries, including contracted projects. However, I think markets are assuming too much demand disappears. Developers can relocate projects, although that takes time. Meta's Prometheus first phase is already complete. Existing infrastructure and international projects leave considerable demand moving forward. Nvidia's valuation looks increasingly attractive after the recent sell-off. At today's price, Fiscal 2027 consensus EPS of $9.31 implies 20.04x earnings. Fiscal 2028's $15.91 estimate brings that to roughly 12x. Forecasts of $21.34 for Fiscal 2029 and $25.98 for Fiscal 2030 imply 8.74x and 7.19x. Expected EPS growth slows from roughly 95% this year to 71%, then 34% and 22%. Those are demanding forecasts, especially further out. Nevertheless, even, say, a 30% shortfall against Fiscal 2028 consensus leaves $11.14 EPS and a 17.1x multiple. Of course, such a misstep is highly unlikely. Regardless, I find even that multiple reasonable for Nvidia's competitive position. Its net-cash balance sheet supports continued investment. CUDA and its networking platform help customers deploy whole systems efficiently. Earnings growth can support returns without a higher multiple. Better shipment execution could also raise estimates. In any case, there are a number of risks to keep in mind. Hyperscalers could moderate capex if AI returns disappoint. Google and Amazon's (AMZN) custom accelerators threaten some workloads, while AMD (AMD) competes for customers. Memory inflation could exceed current assumptions. Nvidia's enormous expected scale also makes shares sensitive to any disappointment. A strong quarter alone cannot remove those risks. Nvidia stock has a Strong Buy consensus, based on 33 Buy ratings. The average price target of $323.45 implies 73% upside from today's share price. I remain bullish ahead of Q3. Political obstacles can slow construction, but customer deployments suggest the compute shortage persists. Around 12x Fiscal 2028 earnings looks unusually attractive to me. Nvidia can deliver compelling returns through earnings growth, provided customers keep converting their AI ambitions into operating capacity. title: Nvidia vs. Alphabet: The AI Revolution Is Big Enough for Both. Here's the Better Buy. - The Motley Fool
content: Which part of the AI trade is more likely to better serve investors? The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution keeps delivering winning stocks driven by that technology. Since AI encompasses so many niches within tech, it will make numerous investors better off, and the gains will not be limited to just one investment. Nvidia (NVDA -4.27%) and Google's parent company, Alphabet (GOOGL +1.18%) (GOOG +0.73%), are two notable winners. The latest iteration of AI is built on Nvidia's hardware, while Alphabet has long innovated in the field, and the success of its most notable businesses relies heavily on AI. Still, between the two tech stocks, I believe Alphabet may have the slightly brighter future. Here's why. Admittedly, it is difficult to go against Nvidia in any AI race. Its AI accelerators power generative AI, and while other competitors have emerged over time, Nvidia's hardware remains dominant. In the first two quarters of fiscal 2027 (ended July 26), that dominance drove a 96% year-over-year increase in revenue for the company. This is not an anomaly, as the growth of Nvidia's AI accelerator business has been unprecedented in recent years. Amid that growth, the stock has gained 1,460% from its October 2022 low. That gave it the world's largest market cap and a surprisingly modest price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 23, below the S&P 500 average earnings multiple of 26. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Nonetheless, the immediate problem is how the company has driven this growth. Increasingly, Nvidia has loaned money to customers to buy equipment. Should some of them declare bankruptcy, the company could be in for massive write-offs. According to its latest 10-Q filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), 70% of its accounts receivable balance comes from just five customers. Amid that lack of diversification, this is not a concern Nvidia investors should dismiss. In contrast, Alphabet appears poised to benefit from present and future growth, though that comes with some challenges. Since Nvidia's 2022 low, Alphabet stock has risen by a more modest 190%. Moreover, its $160 billion in capital expenditures (capex) may seem concerning. The free cash outflows during the last two quarters and the sudden need to increase borrowing may worry shareholders who bought Alphabet for its financial stability. Alphabet appears to surpass Nvidia in unrealized growth potential. With that, its spending may be paying off, and one way is in the growth of Google Cloud. Alphabet's overall revenue grew 24% in the first nine months of 2026. However, that pales in comparison to Google Cloud's 84% revenue increase for the same period. Additionally, Google Cloud generates 21% of the company's revenue. In contrast, Nvidia's data center segment accounts for more than 92% of its revenue. Although Alphabet also finances some of its customers, these percentages suggest it is less exposed to this risk than Nvidia. Furthermore, Alphabet's next great revenue stream could come from Waymo, its autonomous driving company. CEO Sundar Pichai believes Waymo could "meaningfully contribute" to the company's revenue as soon as 2027. While this will almost certainly take years to materialize, it is likely not figured into Alphabet's stock price, leaving considerable room for growth. Finally, investors can buy this stock right now for just 15 times earnings. That valuation arguably makes it worth buying on this pullback. Nvidia and Alphabet are both doing their part to power the AI revolution, but while nobody should discount Nvidia's successes, Alphabet's stock seems to offer greater future growth potential. This comes down to two factors: data center exposure and Waymo's growth. Although Alphabet could get hit if some of its customers go bankrupt, its exposure is a small fraction of what Nvidia faces. Moreover, the Waymo growth story has not yet really started, suggesting the Google parent could experience a huge revenue surge in the coming years. Although Nvidia's growth story is probably far from over, Alphabet looks to have more remaining growth potential. Washington | The woman at the centre of the Nvidia spying scandal pitched an AI chips deal to China-based investors, touting her ability to secure the US company’s coveted GPUs and her commercial relationship with Chinese tech giant Alibaba. Early last year, Alice Huang and her business partner, Kang Wei, sought investment for a South-East Asia data centre project worth several hundred million dollars, according to two investors pitched on the deal. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang (centre right) with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, aka Huang Le, at a party in Taipei in June 2024. NYT The pair said they had “no problem securing GPUs” as a key pillar of the deal and cited Alibaba as a client of the project, according to one investor present. Under current US export controls, it is legal for Chinese companies to lease data centre capacity outside the country. But Chinese ownership of these data centre assets, mostly advanced Nvidia GPUs, is not allowed. Alice Huang did not disclose any close relationship with Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang during the investment pitch or in her regular business dealings. The female executive came under scrutiny when it emerged this month that the US believed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who had been recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. US officials this year wrote a memo, based on information from American intelligence, that said the Nvidia boss had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, who has been an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the chipmaker, according to people familiar with the document. Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le, is also a partner at Hexi Private Equity Partners, a fund established in 2010. It stopped updating its annual results in 2022, with many of its fund products wound up, according to Chinese corporate filings. She was briefly registered in 2023 as an executive at Megaspeed, which is under investigation in multiple jurisdictions regarding alleged chip smuggling. The company has strongly denied allegations of any illicit activity involving chips. Nvidia’s chief admitted on Sunday to having an affair two days after the Financial Times reported his alleged romantic relationship. The New York Times first reported that the US believed Jensen Huang had been the target of an espionage campaign by Chinese authorities. Nvidia shares fell 4 per cent in early trading on Monday (Tuesday AEDT) after the chipmaker’s board said it would open an investigation into the reports. The allegation of espionage could not be independently verified by the FT. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Monday that the spy allegation was groundless, describing it as a smear and defamation. Wei, Alice Huang’s business partner, also serves on the board of Guilin Bank, according to corporate records, a state-controlled bank whose majority investor is the province’s transportation authority. Wei could not be reached for comment by telephone and did not respond to a WeChat request for comment. Alice Huang could not be reached for comment by telephone. Her WeChat and email accounts appear to have been deleted. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang have been seen together at a dinner in Shanghai, where Nvidia has its largest China office by headcount, according to a photo seen by the FT. The duo were also photographed together in Hong Kong and California. None of the photos suggest inappropriate relationships, and several are in a group setting. Megaspeed also leaned on its relationship with Alibaba to open doors with investors. Company documents show that Alibaba, via a Singaporean subsidiary called Apex Enterprise Solutions, lent money to Megaspeed, via its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, in June 2024. As part of the agreement, Speedmatrix pledged its entire business as collateral for the loan. Throughout 2024, Megaspeed’s balance sheet grew from $US33 million ($48 million) to $US3 billion, much of which was based on its subsidiaries’ dealings. Alibaba was Megaspeed’s anchor customer for its South-East Asia cloud service since the beginning and has remained its largest client, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. One added that Nvidia first met Megaspeed to discuss potential procurement because the company had shown its leasing contract with Alibaba. Stunning allegations of a spy plot have prompted Nvidia to investigate whether its founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." Huang on Sunday admitted to having an extramarital affair, and acknowledged that news reports surrounding the relationship and potential national security concerns led Nvidia's board to investigate. He and his chipmaking company did not name the person he had been intimate with, but The New York Times identified her as business executive and Chinese citizen Alice Huang. The outlet said U.S. intelligence determined she was gathering information for Beijing. China's Foreign Ministry dismissed the spying allegations on Monday, saying they amount to a smear campaign. Many questions remain unanswered. But the scandal is already bringing turmoil to California-based Nvidia, whose high-end chips have emerged as the leading building blocks for artificial intelligence. Huang himself has become a key face in the AI race, both across the industry and often on President Donald Trump's side in Washington. On Sunday, Nvidia announced that its board was initiating an independent investigation. The company cited recent reporting about Huang being "the target of a foreign intelligence effort." Nvidia's board said it had "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. The company added that Huang would remain CEO — and that he had committed to cooperating fully during the investigation. "Today's news will not slow Nvidia," company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." In a separate email to Nvidia employees, later also published by the company, Huang apologized for his affair. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children," Huang wrote, adding that he was "deeply sorry" and that his colleagues also "deserve better" from him. Huang also reiterated his support for the board's investigation. "I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security," he said Sunday. Huang, 63, founded Nvidia more than three decades ago. He and his wife, Lori, reportedly have two children who both work at Nvidia. China has denied that it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Nvidia's CEO. "The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said during a routine briefing Monday. The New York Times reported that Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia. Last year, Megaspeed faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China — which the company in December maintained there was "no evidence" of. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times. Last month, the outlet reported that U.S. intelligence agencies discovered Nvidia's Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang — and determined she was feeding information directly to Beijing. Beyond rising to fame in the AI space (often accompanied by his signature leather jacket), Huang has maintained a close relationship to Trump throughout the Republican president's second term in office. He's among tech CEOs who have dined at the White House, and even traveled on Air Force One. Trump has called Huang "smart" and "amazing," repeatedly insisting he accompany him on foreign trips. After news of Nvidia's investigation broke, the president said on Sunday the two hadn't spoken but that he hoped "everything's fine." He continued to praise Huang, including when asked whether he wished he had acted on intelligence when he was briefed about spying. "I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. He's done an amazing job for our country," Trump told reporters. He added that he was still open to taking Huang on his trip to Asia next week. Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable companies. And it's become a leader for making chips that power AI. Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning Trump's approval for selling its H200 chips in January. Those are not the company's most cutting-edge chips, but are still powerful. Nvidia has said in regulatory filings that it has sold only a small amount to China, as such sales are also restricted by the Chinese government. Nvidia's investigation into whether Huang was a target of foreign intelligence is still ongoing, but some analysts suspect that the allegations will strengthen calls for stricter export controls with China. "The high-profile nature of these allegations could make it increasingly difficult for Washington to avoid a response," analysts at Raymond James wrote in a Sunday note. They said the espionage reports will likely bolster congressional support for legislation aimed at further restricting semiconductor and chipmaking equipment sales to China, which could in turn renew strain over trade between the two countries overall. Shares of Nvidia sank more than 4% on Monday. Stocks for other AI-related companies, including Advanced Micro Devices and Coreweave, meanwhile climbed higher. AP Writers Rio Yamat, Michelle L. In an email to Nvidia employees, Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized to his family. The company's board has launched an independent investigation into the matter, but noted that it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised." "The issue is that Jensen is the product strategist, the closer with the hyperscalers, and the face of the company in Washington and Beijing. This story puts that last role at risk," Moorehead said. But he wrote that the incident could hurt the CEO's credibility. "Regardless of the outcome of the investigation, however, we necessarily see Jensen losing some of his power/credibility in advocating for AI and Nvidia with US government representatives (whether free trade with foreign entities or how the government regulates AI development)," Bryson wrote. After years of tremendous gains, 2026 is proving to be a much more challenging one for chip giant Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA). Heading into this week, the stock has been flat, and news that CEO Jensen Huang has been involved in an affair with a Chinese spy has sparked new concerns about governance and potential government repercussions. The stock has been struggling mightily of late and may soon hit a new 52-week low. Is Nvidia really in trouble, or is the market overreacting, and could this instead be a great buying opportunity for investors? Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Prior to this week, the big concerns around big tech were that the recent midterm election results might result in greater pushback on data centers and artificial intelligence (AI) spending as a whole. If that happens, then Nvidia, whose chips are front and center in AI development, could see its growth rate fall significantly. Now, however, there are also concerns that Huang's relationship with a Chinese spy might open up a whole new can of worms. The tech company is looking into the matter, and there may be possible blowback from the government as well, which has been highly restrictive of the types of chips that can be sold to China. While there's no doubt that Nvidia's business has experienced tremendous growth due to AI, the market appears to be pricing in greater uncertainty and risk ahead. The big question for investors is whether these risks are exaggerated, and if the stock is worth buying at these reduced levels. Due to Nvidia's decline in value and impressive growth, it's now trading at a forward price-to-earnings multiple of just 12, which is based on analyst expectations. It's an incredibly low price tag for such a top growth stock. However, it also depends on the company continuing to grow at a fast pace. There's some risk here due to that, but overall, I'm not overly concerned about the spying scandal. Any mistake Huang may have made was likely just that -- a mistake; not something worthy of a serious reprimand from either the government or the company itself. Buying the stock on this decline in value could be a great move for long-term investors, as Nvidia's chips remain in high demand and with fantastic margins, the business still looks poised to be a top stock to own for many years to come. The Nvidia (NVDA) story has been led by Jensen Huang since the company's founding in 1993, sketched out on a napkin at a Denny's. Huang's passion for computing chips (first gaming chips, now AI chips) was on display in an endless stream of interviews, in his signing autographs for enthusiastic fans on his world travels, and in his fried chicken dinner with fellow tech titans overseas that went viral. His star power was evident in the curiosity among the crowds at the annual GTC event about which black leather jacket he would wear on stage to pump up the future of AI. The market's infatuation with Nvidia has gone hand in hand with its infatuation with Huang and the technology he pioneered, which helped create one of the world's most valuable companies. Huang is like Nvidia's sun — the center around which the whole show runs. But a fresh scandal involving the most visible CEO in the world has raised a valid question among investors, perhaps for the first time ever. What in the world is Nvidia's succession plan? Does one even exist? "Every high-profile company carries key-person risk, and Nvidia is no exception," FedWatch strategist Ben Emons said. "While Jensen Huang's full cooperation suggests, in my view, that he has little reason to conceal information and likely did not share sensitive data with the alleged spy, the initial cover-up and later disclosures will still likely weigh on investor confidence." Nvidia's board of directors has launched an independent investigation into reports that a woman CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with was allegedly spying on him for the Chinese government. Huang admitted to the affair on Sunday in an email to employees. Nvidia shares fell 5% in early trading on Monday as a dark cloud settled over Nvidia and its once-Teflon CEO's future. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. Huang has never talked about a succession plan publicly. Nor is anything of the sort disclosed in public filings such as proxy statements or the annual report. The only two people on Nvidia's earnings calls are Huang and longtime CFO Colette Kress. The top four leaders on Nvidia's investor relations page all hold the title of executive vice president: Colette Kress, Nick Parker, Debora Shoquist, and Tim Teter. Usually at these levels of leadership, someone being groomed as a CEO successor would also carry the president title alongside their formal title, such as CFO or COO. By all outward indications, Huang has displayed the typical behavior for an ultra-wealthy founder CEO — one that thinks they'll be doing the job forever and won't slow down at all. For these folks, succession planning is usually far down the totem pole. But all of this has to change for Nvidia, and quickly, in light of the crisis Huang has thrust the company into in front of the whole investing world. The investors who have supported Huang for years (and made bank in the process) deserve to know what happens if Nvidia's epicenter gets pulled out from inside the company. No Jensen at the center, and the expectations on Nvidia's next decade change a great deal. "If Jensen decides to step down, Nvidia could turn to Colette Kress for investor credibility, Ian Buck or Bryan Catanzaro for technical vision, or Jay Puri or Debora Shoquist for steady customer and supply leadership," Emons said. Great, now this has to be communicated to investors for the first time in Nvidia's history. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) supplies the most powerful data center graphics processing units (GPUs) in the world, which are the primary chips used to develop and run artificial intelligence (AI) models. Its stock set a fresh record high of $239.24 last month, but it has since declined by 24% (as of the market close on Nov. 5). Investors are concerned the AI infrastructure boom could lose momentum following last week's midterm elections in the U.S., as newly elected Democratic officials in several states have pledged to take a more cautious approach to data centre development and approvals. But investors will get some much needed clarity on the state of AI spending after the stock market closes on Nov. 17, when Nvidia releases its operating results for its fiscal 2027 third quarter (ended Oct. 31). Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » I think Nvidia is likely to tell investors that demand for GPUs continues to exceed supply, which could spark a recovery in its stock, especially given its attractive valuation. Read on. Nvidia recently started shipping its new Vera Rubin data center systems, which include the Rubin GPU, the Vera central processing unit (CPU), and a series of upgraded networking components. It can deliver up to 30 times more performance in certain workloads compared to the equivalent Blackwell Ultra GPU system, which is Nvidia's previous flagship platform. Moreover, Vera Rubin can reduce inference token costs by a whopping 97%. Inference tokens are the text, images, or computer code a model produces in response to a prompt, so Vera Rubin could make deploying AI software significantly more affordable. This might lead to an increase in AI adoption, while making data center operators more profitable, thus potentially spurring even more demand for chips. In May, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang said every frontier AI company planned to adopt Vera Rubin at launch, which wasn't the case for Blackwell Ultra, so these new systems are likely to be a much bigger commercial success. At a summit in Scotland during September, Huang expanded on his comments, telling the media that Nvidia could sell twice as many chips next year compared to this year. Nvidia doesn't disclose exactly how many chips it sells annually, but it's forecasting overall revenue growth of 70% during its next fiscal year. Wall Street is estimating the company will generate around $411 billion in revenue during its current 2027 fiscal year (according to Yahoo! Finance), which means it could bring in almost $700 billion next year. But all of those forecasts were issued prior to the recent midterm elections, so investors will be eager to hear whether anything has changed, and they should get some clarity on Nov. 17. The risk of a slowdown in infrastructure spending is real. On Nov. 3, constituents in 45 communities across America voted to restrict the building of new data centers in some form, while just one community voted to approve construction. Texas Governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, plans to pause new data center approvals in the state until new laws are established to protect communities from issues like soaring electricity prices and water scarcity. According to Cleanview, over 80 data centers are already operating in Texas, with 50 more under construction, and another 120 planned, so the state is one of America's top destinations for AI infrastructure. Therefore, it's no surprise Nvidia stock has pulled back since the elections. It's hard to predict how the company's GPU sales will be affected in the near term given so much infrastructure is already under construction not just in the U.S., but also around the world. However, I think Nvidia's valuation is starting to appropriately reflect the risks at hand, which means its stock could be a great buy on the dip. Nvidia stock is trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 22.9, a hefty discount to its 10-year average of 61.2. It's also significantly cheaper than the Nasdaq-100 index which has a P/E of 29.9, so it looks heavily undervalued compared to a group of its big-tech peers. I think the sharp decline in Nvidia stock has priced in a potential slowdown in sales, so a fierce rebound might be in order if the company's third-quarter results are positive on Nov. 17, particularly if they are accompanied by some optimistic commentary from Jensen Huang. If he reiterates his original prediction that chip sales will double next year, it will be a sign that he doesn't expect the recent elections to affect demand -- at least in the near term. The PRICE of GOLD rose on Monday amid a weaker US Dollar and falling crude oil prices following last week's 'blue wave' midterms election results, while some AI-related shares recovered from last week's tech sell-off, writes Atsuko Whitehouse at BullionVault. Giant AI chipmaker Nvidia (Nasdaq: NVDA) slid however in US pre-market trading after CEO Jensen Huang was accused of dating a Chinese government spy, while protests against data centres continued in Europe over the weekend. Gold last week gained 3.5%, rebounding from end-October's 13-month low after the US midterm elections resulted in the Democrat Party winning control of both the Senate and the House, but paring gains Friday following stronger-than-expected US jobs data. The Nasdaq Composite ended the week 3.4% lower, its fourth consecutive weekly decline, despite rallying 1.1% on Friday after Thursday's steep tech stock sell-off. The Democrats' sweeping victory in the midterms mean concerns about tighter regulation of AI and data centres "hit a market already nervous on AI capex", says Nicky Shiels, head of metals strategy at Swiss gold bullion refining and finance group MKS Pamp. Bloomberg Opinion columnist John Authers points to investor concerns that the US midterm election results could "make it harder to build AI data centers." By the close on 6 November, the Nasdaq Composite was 10.9% below its 6 October all-time closing high. Over the same period, gold fell 2.6% in US Dollar terms, based on the LBMA's London afternoon auction benchmark. Gold also fell in the early stages of the Dot-Com bust in 2000, though by far less than the Nasdaq Composite. In the 5 weeks after New Year's tech-stock index peaked on 10 March 2000, the Nasdaq fell 34.2%, while gold slipped 2.8%. By the time the Nasdaq Composite reached its Tech Crash closing low on 9 October 2002, the index was down 77.9% from its peak, while gold traded 10.0% above its level on 10 March 2000. Spot gold prices for London settlement today rose as much as 2.1% to $4134 per troy ounce in early Asian trading, peaking below Friday's near-3-week high before easing to $4085 and then rising again to $4115 by lunchtime in the UK, some 1.6% above Friday's afternoon auction price. The Dollar Index – a measure of the US currency's value versus its major rich-world peers – slipped 0.4%, curbing the gains in gold for UK and Euro investors. Brent crude oil meanwhile fell 2.0% to $96.29 a barrel as traders weighed diplomatic efforts to end the US-Iran conflict, extending last week's 16% drop, its steepest since the Covid Crash of April 2020. Most Asian stock markets rose on Monday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 gaining 2.3% for its first rise in six sessions. But South Korea's tech-heavy Kospi fell 0.8% to its lowest close since 2 February, leaving it 44.9% below its June record high, even as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix edged higher. Nvidia shares fell 4.5% in premarket trading after the company responded to media reports of an extra-marital affair by opening an internal investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence 'honey trap' operation. Finding increasing demand from the electrical and electronics industries, silver today rose as much as 2.8% to $53.46 per troy ounce before easing to $52.64, still 1.2% above Friday's London auction price. Silver prices gained 3.8% last week, recovering from a nearly 13-month low in US Dollar terms, but fellow electrical-and-electronics metal copper fell 2.7% on the London Metal Exchange, rallying on Monday as investors weigh the risk of a slowdown in US or European data centre construction. LME three-month copper has now lost over 7.0% since hitting a record $14,875 per tonne on 10 September. title: Nvidia Stock Drops 5%: What the Jensen Huang Investigation Means for NVDA - Coinpedia
content: Nvidia (NVDA) stock fell 5.7% in premarket trading on Monday, November 9, slipping below $180.30 as fresh controversy surrounding CEO Jensen Huang unsettled investors. The decline adds to recent pressure on the AI chip giant, with concerns over leadership uncertainty emerging at a time when semiconductor stocks are already facing heightened volatility. While Nvidia remains a dominant force in artificial intelligence, the latest developments introduce a new risk for shareholders. Could the investigation trigger a deeper NVDA price sell-off, or will investors look beyond the controversy? The immediate trigger is Nvidia’s board decision to investigate reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The company announced on November 8 that a committee of independent directors, supported by external legal counsel, would oversee the review. The investigation follows reports involving Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company connected to Nvidia’s AI chip business. Huang separately acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees and apologized to his family and colleagues. He has committed to cooperating with the board’s investigation. Importantly, Nvidia said it currently has no reason to believe that national security or company secrets were compromised. The board also expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team. The investigation matters because Huang is closely associated with Nvidia’s transformation into a dominant force in artificial intelligence. Under his leadership, Nvidia expanded beyond graphics processors into AI accelerators, data-center infrastructure and the CUDA software ecosystem. His relationships with major technology customers and policymakers have also played an important role in the company’s expansion. Any uncertainty surrounding his position could therefore affect investor confidence beyond the immediate controversy. The situation also puts Nvidia’s China strategy under renewed scrutiny. Washington has imposed restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports to China, making the company’s commercial relationships and technology safeguards particularly sensitive. Nvidia’s near-term outlook now depends on whether the investigation can resolve concerns without disrupting its leadership or business operations. A review that finds no compromise of company information could help investors refocus on AI demand, data-center growth and the upcoming earnings report. However, prolonged scrutiny or uncertainty surrounding Huang’s position could keep NVDA shares volatile. If NVDA stock sustains above $170, it may see a reversal toward $185-$190. However, a break below $165 could trigger a major fall toward $150. The November 17 earnings report may provide an important counterweight to the controversy. Strong revenue growth and forward guidance could reinforce confidence in Nvidia’s underlying business, while weaker expectations could amplify existing concerns. title: NVDA Stock On Track To Hit 5-Month Low, $200B Wipeout: Yale Professor Sees 50/50 Chance Jensen Huang Keeps CEO Job - Stocktwits
content: Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld sees the odds of Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang keeping his job at roughly 50-50, pointing to a history of corporate leaders who lost their positions after personal scandals. “I think it's about a 50-50 chance,” Sonnenfeld said in an interview with CNBC on Monday. According to him, previous CEO departures were not necessarily driven by public disapproval of infidelity, but by concerns about trust and disclosure. “It wasn't because we are so puritanical a nation and culture that we're so worried about the infidelities and the frailties of human nature,” he said. “But it's when they deceive the board that we have the problem.” NVDA stock dropped as much as 4.5% in pre-market trade on Monday, on track to hit a five-month low, wipe out over $200 billion of its market capitalization if losses hold through the day, and was the top trending ticker on Stocktwits at the time of writing. According to Sonnenfeld, the board’s assessment of what Huang knew, when he knew it, and what he disclosed could be more important than the personal relationship alone. He pointed to the confidence Huang has built over more than three decades leading Nvidia, including support from prominent business leaders. Sonnenfeld called the current situation a serious test of that standing. He said Huang had been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” but characterized the episode as “remarkably poor judgment.” “Any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” he said, adding that the recklessness alone could mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.” Sonnenfeld pointed out that even if the board considers a leadership change, it is uncertain if Nvidia has an obvious internal successor ready to take over. He noted that while Nvidia has several strong senior executives, including its chief financial officer and chief operating officer, “none of them have ever led a public company” or have Huang’s visibility. “I don't see any one of them being able to step in here in a time of crisis,” Sonnenfeld said of the company’s board members. Sonnenfeld said several high-profile companies have removed CEOs after investigations into relationships, workplace conduct, or questions about executive disclosure. At McDonald’s (MCD), Steve Easterbrook was fired in November 2019 after the board found he had engaged in a consensual relationship with an employee, violating company policy. The company later alleged that Easterbrook had concealed additional relationships and misled investigators, leading McDonald’s to seek the return of his severance package. Intel (INTC) CEO Brian Krzanich resigned in June 2018 after the company found that a past consensual relationship with an employee violated its non-fraternization policy. Norfolk Southern (NSC) removed CEO Alan Shaw in September 2024 after an investigation found he had engaged in a relationship with the company’s chief legal officer, violating its policies. Meanwhile, Best Buy (BBY) CEO Brian Dunn resigned in 2012 following a board investigation into his relationship with a female employee. At L-3 Communications, now part of L3Harris (LHX), Chris Kubasik resigned in 2012 after disclosing a relationship with a subordinate while he was president and CEO-elect. Sonnenfeld also noted former Hewlett-Packard (HP) CEO Mark Hurd, who resigned in 2010 after a board investigation into expense-report inaccuracies following a sexual-harassment complaint. The investigation did not substantiate the harassment allegations. “That’s what happened with Mark Hurd and Hewlett Packard,” Sonnenfeld said, adding that in previous cases “the board didn't have full information, or there was some element of deceit.” Hurd’s departure also illustrates that leaving a CEO role does not necessarily end an executive’s career. Oracle (ORCL) hired him as co-president about a month after he left HP. Platform data showed an over 800% jump in message volume. However, Chinese intelligence has denied any such reports. Some traders on Stocktwits debated that the controversy had little bearing on Nvidia’s underlying business and said they would consider buying more shares if the stock continued to fall. NVDA stock is down over 1% for the year, not accounting for the pre-market slide. title: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with alleged Chinese spy - CNBC
content:
Nvidia has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. U.S. intelligence agencies have expressed concerns that the woman, Alice Huang, who is affiliated with a cloud company and an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and the Financial Times. Huang told Nvidia staff in an email on Sunday that he had an affair with the woman and that Nvidia’s board of directors had opened an independent investigation into the spying allegations. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” Huang wrote in the message. “I am deeply sorry.” An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption. In a statement, the Nvidia board said it would investigate the allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” Nvidia’s board said in a statement. Read Huang’s email to Nvidia employees and the company board of directors’ statement here. The allegations come as Nvidia has become the center of a trade dispute between China and the U.S. as AI is seen as increasingly critical to national security. The U.S. restricts exports of Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips to China, though it has approved exports of certain older, slower models. Megaspeed, which Ms. Huang is affiliated with, has been accused of helping restricted Chinese companies acquire Nvidia AI chips. Nvidia representatives previously said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls. Nvidia’s Huang has pushed for broader AI chip exports to China, saying it is better for the U.S. if the world uses and builds on American technology. He has also aligned with President Donald Trump on American artificial intelligence policy and its infrastructure buildout. In his note to staff, Huang said he was “proud and grateful” to be an American. Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18.
